publications.summary: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the financial industry as well as the broader economy, creating both opportunities and risks. Banks and asset managers, which represent key channels of financial intermediation in the euro area, are increasingly using AI for tasks such as credit scoring, fraud detection and portfolio management. publications.summary: A new wave of equity issuance, concentrated in AI-related sectors, has brought public equity financing back to the forefront of capital markets. SpaceX’s record initial public offering (IPO) has led the way, with OpenAI and Anthropic planning to follow. This special feature assesses the financial stability implications of large IPOs and equity issuance in general, as well as how these interact with the trend towards passive investing. Primary equity financing supports financial stability by absorbing losses and limiting leverage at the firm level, but aggregate equity issuance is highly cyclical and strongly influenced by investor sentiment.

Monetary policy, segmented capital markets and innovation
publications.summary: We identify a novel mechanism linking monetary policy, innovation, and capital-market segmentation. When capital markets are imperfectly integrated, contractionary monetary policy tightens the financing constraints of externally financed firms, amplifying the decline in innovation induced by tighter financial conditions; monetary easing operates in reverse. Using granular euro-area firm-level data on balance sheets and patenting, matched with bank-level and credit-registry information, we show that monetary policy affects innovation through financing constraints. The effects are strongest for firms with high intangible intensity and for firms operating in AI-related sectors.

The macroeconomic effects of defence spending: what impact beyond GDP?
publications.summary: This paper estimates the macroeconomic effects of defence spending for a panel of up to 27 EU member states over 1999–2025 using Panel Local Projections. We look beyond the output multiplier that dominates the literature to trace the price implications of defence spending and the demand-side channels through which effects operate. A key methodological contribution is a country-specific order-date adjustment for capital expenditure, constructed from the SIPRI Arms Transfers Database, which shifts the estimated (unitary) peak GDP multiplier from around year one to approximately year three to four. Under this specification, the HICP inflation response is higher and occurs earlier.

Unlocking supervisory effectiveness in credit risk: insights from the ECB’s supervisory findings and measures
publications.summary: This paper provides an assessment of supervisory effectiveness in credit risk using confidential data from ECB Banking Supervision. The analysis covers 8,106 supervisory measures issued and closed between 2016 and 2025. A central contribution is the construction of a measure level indicator of supervisory effectiveness based on large language model (LLM) analysis of supervisory narratives and closure justifications. The indicator captures whether supervisory measures resulted in full remediation of the underlying deficiencies. Using logistic and duration models, we examine the characteristics of findings, measures, and banks associated with remediation outcomes and remediation speed.

Deep-π*: a neural network estimate of trend inflation
publications.summary: Most empirical models of trend inflation treat it as a latent random walk driven by unobserved shocks, so they cannot say which economic conditions move it. Deep- π*makes the innovations to the trend a possibly nonlinear function of a large number of macroeconomic indicators, estimated with neural networks, so that Shapley values can be used to attribute every movement of the trend to the indicators behind it. Two complementary loss functions define a current trend, which fits inflation today, and a forward-looking trend, which best predicts inflation over the next year. In US data, employment-related variables were the largest contributors to the post-pandemic rise of the current trend.

publications.summary: Government spending effectiveness depends critically on how it is financed. publications.title: Elastic in cash, inelastic in repo: hedge funds in the treasury and repo markets
publications.summary: The functioning of sovereign bond markets is closely intertwined with repo markets, where investors finance long positions and source bonds for short sales. We show, theoretically and empirically, how conditions in the cash bond market fundamentally shape repo rates: When demand for cash bonds exceeds available supply, arbitrageurs, notably hedge funds, step in to bridge the gap by shorting bonds and borrowing them in the repo market. These arbitrage strategies drive a wedge between monetary policy rates and repo rates, generating “specialness”.

publications.summary: We study how frictions impact haircut setting in repo markets. Using transaction-level supervisory data and exploiting the 2021 introduction of the binding leverage ratio requirement, we show that three frictions jointly shape haircuts in the bilateral dealer-to-client segment: dealer balance sheet constraints, collateral convenience yields, and client outside options. In collateral-driven repos, binding leverage constraints and broader client outside options both raise haircuts, while higher convenience yields push them down.

publications.title: When less is more: behavioral effects of CBDC holding limits
publications.summary: Holding limits are a central design feature of proposed retail central bank digital currencies (CBDC). While such limits mechanically prevent individuals from exceeding a maximum balance, they may also generate behavioral responses whose directions are a priori unclear. We conducted an incentivized online experiment with participants from four euro-area countries, exogenously varying the presence and level of a holding limit to causally separate direct mechanical effects from behavioral effects. We find that behavioral responses increase holdings of the means of payment subject to the holding limit, consistent with an attraction effect.

publications.summary: Monetary policy tightening generates valuation losses on banks’ securities portfolios, reducing the collateral available for interbank borrowing. These effects were strongest for banks with limited liquidity buffers and high collateral utilisation.

publications.title: Monetary policy under multiple financing constraints
publications.summary: The fact that monetary policy tightening has stronger effects than easing is a longstanding puzzle in monetary economics. This article studies monetary transmission in settings where firms face multiple financing constraints – a common and well-documented feature of corporate financing. Our theory shows that the multiplicity of financing constraints notably dampens the transmission of expansionary policy to firm borrowing and investment, while amplifying the transmission of policy tightening. This asymmetry arises because, when policy tightens, the most responsive constraint binds; whereas, when policy eases, the least responsive constraint limits the expansion of borrowing.

publications.title: Monetary policy transmission through cross-selling banks
publications.summary: Banks trade off short-term losses on deposits against long-term profits from cross-selling other products to new depositors. This strategy is especially attractive when policy rates are low and future sales are more valuable. Therefore, deposit rates move less than policy rates: banks keep them relatively higher when policy rates fall, and relatively lower when policy rates rise. As returns on other financial assets follow policy rates more closely, this makes deposits relatively less attractive for depositors at higher policy rates. Therefore, policy rate hikes lead to a reduction in deposits, which are the key source of refinancing for bank loans.

publications.summary: We present novel empirical evidence on lending practices across all euro area countries, using AnaCredit data covering nearly seven million new loans issued to non-financial corporations in 2022-23. We document substantial variation in (a) the prevalence of fixed versus floating-rate loans, (b) rate fixation periods, and (c) reference rates. This variation results in lending rates being exposed to different segments of the risk-free rate yield curve which, in turn, influences their sensitivity to monetary policy changes. We show that loans priced using shorter-term relevant risk-free rates experience more pronounced monetary pass-through.

publications.title: Authorities complete 2026 review of payments Memorandum of Understanding
publications.summary: The Bank of England (the Bank), Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and Payment Systems Regulator (PSR) have completed their annual review of the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on payments. Read the MoU (PDF)Outcome of the review: The review found that cooperation and coordination between the Authorities – the Bank, FCA, PRA and PSR – has strengthened and remains effective. We concluded that no changes to the MoU are needed at this time. To complement the MoU, we have updated our information explaining how our objectives, regulatory remits and key workstreams fit together.

publications.title: Bereaved families need support, not a battle with paperwork
publications.summary: Investment firms must do more to help people dealing with the death of a loved one, after a review found confusing communications, delays and gaps in support. The FCA reviewed how financial advisers, wealth managers and investment platforms support bereaved families and those handling someone’s estate. Some firms provided thoughtful, personal support. Others had processes that risked adding to people’s distress and financial pressure. Some firms left people unclear about what to do next or offered limited ways to get in touch. In some cases, advice fees were still being taken until an original death certificate was provided.

publications.title: Check the firm before you invest, FCA warns, as AI scams rise
publications.summary: A third (33%) of UK adults say they have seen an investment promotion in the past year that they believe used artificial intelligence (AI), new research from the FCA shows. Reports of investment fraud to Report Fraud that mention suspected use of AI have risen by nearly 400% in a year, up from 193 in 2024/25 to 956 in 2025/26. Investment fraud victims lost an average of £28,188 in 2025/26. Most people feel confident they could spot an AI investment scam, but that confidence is lower when a well-known person is involved. Almost two-thirds (62%) of adults say they could identify an investment scam that used AI.

publications.title: Cyber resilience: building confidence as threats evolve
publications.summary: Speech by Mark Francis, director of specialists at the Cyber Security in Financial Services Summit. There is no shortage of material for a speech about cyber security at the moment. Recent months have provided some stark reminders of just how interconnected our digital economy has become. Major outages affecting Microsoft and Google have shown how problems in one part of the system can reverberate widely. We are seeing that changing environment reflected in our own data too. Last month was the highest month for cyber incidents reported to the FCA in the past 18 months, and the second highest in the past 5 years. And those numbers sit against a broader shift in the operating environment.

publications.title: FCA charges individual with money laundering
publications.summary: The FCA has charged Raymond Fieldhouse with a money laundering offence. Mr Fieldhouse is accused of laundering over £1.42m made from investment scams between 1 June 2017 and 1 August 2018. Mr Fieldhouse appeared at Stockport Magistrates’ Court on 17 November 2026 where he did not enter a plea. He was remanded in custody until his plea and trial preparation hearing on 22 December 2026 at Southwark Crown Court. Notes to editorsRaymond Fieldhouse was born on 29 April 1982. His nationality is British/Venezuelan. Mr Fieldhouse is accused of money laundering, contrary to section 327 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002. Fighting financial crime is a priority in the FCA’s 5-year strategy.

publications.title: FCA launches world-first platform giving firms new insight into AI innovation
publications.summary: New resource brings together real-world examples of AI adoption across financial services, helping firms identify emerging trends and opportunities. The FCA has launched a world-first AI Spotlight Observatory that provides firms, academics and innovators with a comprehensive view of how AI is being adopted across financial services. Based on practical use cases from more than 200 organisations and spanning 150 areas of activity, the online platform highlights how firms are using AI across the industry and where trends are developing.

publications.title: FCA proposes greater pension investment flexibility to support long-term value for savers
publications.summary: Workplace pension providers could have greater flexibility to invest for the long term under proposals from the FCA, helping them deliver better outcomes for savers while ensuring savers' interests remain protected. The FCA is consulting on excluding certain performance-linked fees from the charge cap for default funds in workplace pensions it regulates. Performance-linked fees are common in private markets, including private equity, venture capital and private credit. The proposed change would give providers greater flexibility to access a broader range of investments where this could help improve long-term returns and value for savers.

publications.title: Geordie Shore star and illegal finfluencer sentenced for promoting high-risk investments on social media
publications.summary: Aaron Chalmers, a reality TV star and social media content creator, and finfluencer Jason Agbodza have been sentenced for illegally promoting an unauthorised foreign exchange trading scheme on social media. Chalmers, 39 and from Newcastle, was sentenced at City of London Magistrates Court. He previously pleaded guilty and today (19 November) was fined £3,072 and ordered to pay costs of £2,836. Having risen to fame on Geordie Shore, Chalmers has more than 2 million followers on Instagram. Agbodza, 35, of London, was also fined £1,173 and ordered to pay costs of £2,114 after pleading guilty.

publications.title: Getting the full picture of trading in UK shares
publications.summary: Why a complete picture mattersIn today’s market, firms can choose where and how they trade. Previous analysis has found that this competitive landscape benefits firms in wholesale markets. However, trading in UK shares has become more dispersed across venues and different ways of executing trades. Better information about market-wide activity helps firms assess liquidity, make investment decisions and understand trading costs. However, obtaining a complete picture of that activity has become more difficult. As we set out in CP26/30, overall trading activity in UK equity markets has been robust over recent years (see figure 1).

publications.title: Helping more people break the cycle of persistent credit card debt
publications.summary: Credit cards are a useful financial tool for many – offering flexibility and helping people manage spending and cash flow. But if customers only make low repayments over a long period, they can end up in debt for years while racking up interest and charges. The persistent debt rules we introduced in 2018 aimed to tackle this. They said that lenders had to identify customers who, over an 18-month period, paid more in interest, fees and charges than towards their balance. Lenders had to contact these customers and encourage them to increase repayments if they could afford it, and if they were still struggling, lenders had to take additional steps to help them repay their balances sustainably.

publications.title: How should investors evaluate performance?
publications.summary: Why fund performance needs a detailed review in concentrated marketsA fund’s headline return tells only part of the story. Before selling a fund that has underperformed its benchmark, investors should ask why and whether it still meets their needs. This matters when a small group of companies dominate stock market returns. A fund that spreads its investments more widely may underperform a concentrated index. That does not necessarily mean its manager has made poor decisions. Equally, diversification should not become an excuse for weak stock picking. There could also be a big impact on pensions, which play a vital role in people’s financial futures.

publications.title: Insurance firms called on to improve claims handling
publications.summary: The FCA and Financial Ombudsman Service have published a report setting out what insurers need to focus on to ensure claims are dealt with promptly, clearly and fairly. We are helping firms learn from Financial Ombudsman complaints and strengthen their claims handling in line with our existing rules to improve service quality for insurance customers. The report highlights where claims handling can improve and explains the key rules firms need to meet. Building on findings in our 2025 review of home and travel insurance, it calls on insurers to:Keep claims moving. Give customers clear and timely updates. Take responsibility when problems arise with third parties working on their behalf.

publications.title: Kandoo Car Credit Ltd enters administration
publications.summary: On 19 November 2026, Kandoo Car Credit Ltd (Kandoo) was placed into administration. Steve Kenny and Richard Cole of KBL Advisory Limited were appointed as joint administrators. Kandoo Car Credit (firm reference number 936619) operated as a motor finance credit broker arranging finance for consumers purchasing vehicles from third-party car dealerships. The joint administrators, Steve Kenny and Richard Cole of KBL Advisory Ltd, are now responsible for Kandoo while it is in administration. If you have questions about the administration or a claim against Kandoo, contact the joint administrators. Email: kandoo.queries@kbl-advisory.comKandoo is no longer arranging finance.

publications.title: Man sentenced over £154m fake takeover bid targeting UK-listed company
publications.summary: Christopher Woolcott has today been given a 2-year prison sentence, suspended for 2 years, after staging a £154m fake takeover bid for Touchstone Exploration Inc. He was also ordered to complete 200 hours of unpaid work and to pay costs of £4,627.73. Mr Woolcott built a sizeable stake in Touchstone, an oil and gas listed company. He then launched a bogus bid to drive up its share price. To give the bid credibility, Mr Woolcott invented several identities, forged takeover documents using Chat GPT and met Touchstone’s chief executive at a central London hotel under a false name. Touchstone ultimately determined that the bid was not legitimate.

publications.title: Motor finance compensation scheme calculation
publications.summary: While preparing our response to the legal challenges to our motor finance redress scheme, we identified some errors in how we categorised a small group of loan agreements. This data informed the annual percentage rate (APR) adjustment we use in our calculation of compensation. We set this at 17% for agreements from 1 April 2014. Our initial work to understand the impact of the errors suggests that, if there is any impact, this would be less than 1 percentage point either side of 17%. While the potential impact on average compensation is small – less than £10 per agreement, on average – we recognise this affects the ongoing litigation. We properly informed those challenging the scheme.

publications.title: Smarter regulation means understanding the trade-offs
publications.summary: Regulation inevitably involves choices. Protecting consumers and maintaining confidence in our markets are fundamental to what we do. But rules also have costs. They can affect businesses’ decisions to invest, innovate and compete. Good regulation means recognising those trade-offs and using evidence to decide where intervention will make the biggest difference. That is why economics matters so much to good regulation. At our annual Economics Conference, economists, academics, regulators and industry experts came together to explore how smarter financial regulation can support sustainable growth and innovation.

publications.title: The courage to change
publications.summary: Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at TheCityUK National Conference 2026. Our willingness to do things differently in this country has helped make our financial services sector one of the most innovative in the world. We didn’t get here by accident. It took ambitious firms, given the right amount of room to experiment. The FCA recognised the importance of pushing the boundaries with Project Innovate in 2014. And the world’s first Regulatory Sandbox in 2016, allowing firms to test innovative ideas with dedicated FCA support. By 2024, fintech was the most significant job source in UK financial services.

publications.title: The EBA consults on revised technical standards for the reclassification of investment firms as credit institutions
publications.summary: The European Banking Authority (EBA) today launched a consultation on three draft Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) on the reclassification of investment firms as credit institutions, when they exceed the EUR 30 billion total assets threshold. The proposals clarify how total assets should be calculated against this threshold, how investment firms should report this information to competent authorities, and the conditions under which competent authorities can decide to grant a waiver. The revised RTS reflect the 2024 amendments to the Capital Requirements Directive (CRD) and contribute to a more proportionate and risk-based application of the framework for investment firms.

publications.title: The not-so-fine print: making consumer contracts fair
publications.summary: How many of us read the terms and conditions of a contract before buying a financial product? Contracts hold the detail that shapes everyone's financial life, whether you're taking out a loan, insuring your holiday, or signing up for a crypto wallet. All firms are responsible for making sure that terms in their consumer contracts comply with the fairness and transparency requirements of the Consumer Rights Act (CRA) 2015. When those terms don’t comply, our Consumer Contracts team has powers to challenge firms directly. This work shows how we use the full range of powers Parliament has given us, not only those in financial services legislation, to tackle harm.

publications.title: UK financial watchdogs clarify cyber expectations as attacks rise
publications.summary: UK’s financial regulators are proposing new guidance to help financial services firms prepare for and recover from cyber incidents as threats grow. The Bank of England’s most recent Systemic Risk Survey cited cyber as one of the risks that would have the greatest impact on the UK financial system. October 2026 saw the second-highest monthly number of cyber incidents reported to the FCA in 5 years, and the highest in the past 18 months, 52% above the previous high recorded in May 2025.

publications.title: What we’re learning from firms engaging with our innovation services
publications.summary: Three themes stand out: the growing use of AI, innovation crossing traditional sector boundaries, and financial inclusion. As firms develop new products, services and business models, many engage with us through our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways to understand how regulation applies to their proposition or to test innovative ideas in a controlled environment. Looking across applications lets us observe emerging trends. It helps us understand how technologies are evolving, and identify emerging regulatory questions. In turn, this supports our wider work and helps us keep pace with developments across financial services.
